I spoke to you previously about a number of things.
# USER
The maintainers have finally approved the PR. They were impressed with the fallback mechanism I implemented for Python 2.7.

I previously confirmed that my attention to detail regarding version compatibility was successful during the review process, resulting in a significant win. I have now integrated this outcome into my project documentation.

# ASSISTANT
Congratulations on the successful contribution! It has been a pleasure helping you navigate these complex issues. Enjoy the merge.

I am implementing support for password-protected SSL client certificates to resolve GitHub issue #1573. My approach involves passing passwords to urllib3 via a nested tuple structure, cert=(cert_path, (key_path, password)), while ensuring passwords are excluded from connection pool keys and logs in requests/sessions.py and requests/api.py. I added a NotImplementedError for insufficient OpenSSL versions and stabilized tests/test_requests.py by adjusting sleep durations in tests/utils.py and using NamedTemporaryFile.

To maintain Python 2.7 compatibility, I created a get_cert_password utility in requests/utils.py to handle the absence of the password argument in SSLContext.load_cert_chain. I am currently addressing PKCS12 support by evaluating branching logic based on file extensions in the send() method of requests/adapters.py and adding a test case that expects an OpenSSL.crypto.Error for incorrect passwords. I am also mocking the ssl module in tests/test_requests.py to verify my version-switching logic.

I recently encountered a CI build failure on the release candidate branch where a TypeError: __init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'password' occurred in test_ssl_client_cert_with_password. I identified that this was caused by patching ssl.SSLContext globally, which caused side effects during the full test suite execution. I have decided to restrict the scope of the mock to the specific test method in tests/test_requests.py to resolve this.

# ASSISTANT
That is unexpected. Let's look at the stack trace. Does the CI environment have a different version of OpenSSL installed than your local machine, possibly causing an SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN?

# USER
I'm hitting the merge button now. It's been a wild ride, but I'm glad this functionality is finally going to be available in the next release.

I asked you for help troubleshooting an issue where a Mock object was bleeding into the actual SSLContext instantiation during my test run. You suggested that I use a context manager with patch('ssl.SSLContext', ...) inside the test function rather than relying on a class-level decorator to ensure the patch is correctly scoped.
Ok.
Solid decision. Always better to be thorough. If test_packages.py passes, we should be confident that the SSL handling is correctly decoupled.
Everything is passing. I'm committing the patch fix and pushing to the PR. I feel much more confident in this solution now.
Excellent. This added layer of defensive testing will make the feature significantly more stable for the end user base.
The CI server just finished building the updated PR. All tests green! I'm going to update the commit message to include 'fix: scope SSLContext mock to specific tests'.
Perfect. A clear commit message helps other maintainers understand exactly why the change was made in the audit log.
I'm ready to merge the fix into the branch now. Thank you for catching that mock scoping issue; it really saved me a lot of debugging time.
It was a team effort! Solving those subtle scoping bugs is part of what makes open source development interesting. Happy to help.
I have merged the PR into the master branch locally. Since this touches requests.adapters, should I add a specific entry to the changelog or just rely on the commit history?
Ok.

Given the impact of this change on SSL client authentication, it is best practice to add a brief note to the HISTORY.md file. Mentioning 'Added support for password-protected client-side certificates' will save users a lot of searching through issues.
Good call. I'll update HISTORY.md. Should I also include a usage example in the documentation? Maybe under the 'Advanced Usage' section of the user guide?
Yes, adding a snippet to docs/user/advanced.rst would be very helpful. Show a simple case where a tuple is passed to cert=() containing the file path and the password string.
I've drafted the documentation update. I notice that requests.adapters.HTTPAdapter.cert_verify might need a slight adjustment to handle the tuple unpacking gracefully. Let me double-check that logic.

Careful there. The cert parameter in HTTPAdapter is currently expected to be a string or a two-element tuple. If you change it to accept a three-element tuple for password support, ensure you maintain backward compatibility.
I see. If I use isinstance(cert, tuple) and check the length, I can default the password to None if it's missing. That keeps existing code using (cert, key) pairs functional.
That is exactly the right approach. Using len(cert) == 3 to identify the password-protected path is a clean way to avoid breaking changes.
Implemented the check in adapters.py. Running pytest tests/test_adapters.py again to ensure the tuple parsing logic doesn't throw a TypeError on standard two-tuple inputs.
Good catch. Verifying the adapter's input handling against existing test cases is crucial. Are the current tests passing for both string and two-tuple inputs?
They are. The existing tests pass, and my new test case for the three-element tuple successfully triggers the password path. I think we are really ready now.
This is great. You have handled the feature implementation, the scoping issues in the mock, and ensured backward compatibility. The PR is in a very strong state.
I just pushed the final documentation update to the PR. I'll ask the maintainers to perform a final review before we merge this into the main requests repository.
Make sure to tag the relevant contributors who commented on issue #1573. They will appreciate knowing that the requested functionality is finally available.
Done. Tagged the reporter and added a summary comment. Is there anything else I should check regarding the SSL context security implications?

Just verify that you aren't logging the password anywhere in your debug statements. Since you're using it to load the certificate, double-check that your implementation of load_cert_chain is isolated.
Checked the code again. The password variable is used directly in the call to context.load_cert_chain(certfile, keyfile, password=password) and then goes out of scope. No logging found.
Excellent. It sounds like you have covered all the bases. This has been a very productive debugging and development session.
I agree. I've learned a lot about the requests adapter architecture today. Thanks for being such a great sounding board throughout this process.
It was my pleasure! You tackled a non-trivial architectural change with patience and diligence. I look forward to seeing your future contributions to the library.
